strengths: Timely and critical inquiry into bioimaging representation learning: mirrors vital sanity-check efforts recently seen in single-cell transcriptomics by showing that standard benchmark performance often conflates true biological abstraction with low-level shortcuts and architectural priors.

Comprehensive empirical scope: evaluates multiple biological scales (cell culture profiling via RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, JUMP-MoA, and tissue spatial transcriptomics/histopathology via HEST-1k, BRACS, and BACH) across diverse architectures (ResNets, ViTs, DINO, GNNs, EGNNs).

Insightful diagnostic analyses: the layer-wise probing (showing performance degradation or plateaus at deeper layers in contrast to ImageNet), representational dimensionality analysis (linking PCA explained variance to retrieval collapse in ResNets), and rank correlation comparisons provide clear mechanistic explanations for model behaviors.

Well-designed baseline suites: the introduction of pixel statistics, untrained encoders (including a minimal SingleConv), and structure-only representations (rendered cell graphs and point clouds) effectively calibrates benchmark difficulty and exposes the role of confounders such as cell density/count.

Actionable recommendations: provides concrete guidelines for future bioimaging benchmarks, including layer reporting, reporting untrained and low-dimensional proxies, and fine-grained diagnostic breakdowns.
weaknesses: Dependence on upstream cell segmentation for structure-only baselines: the tissue structure graphs rely on nuclear centroids extracted by a pretrained segmentation network (CellViT). Systematic segmentation errors or omissions correlated with cell morphology/staining quality could subtly leak morphological cues into centroid locations.

Nuance regarding state-of-the-art in-domain foundation models: while untrained baselines match general-purpose vision backbones on RxRx3-core, proprietary large in-domain models (MAE-G/8) and pathology foundation models (H-Optimus-1) demonstrate substantial gains over baselines on multiple benchmarks. The overarching narrative occasionally risks sounding overly pessimistic relative to what large-scale in-domain models actually achieve.

Disentangling cell count from higher-order spatial structure: as noted in the discussion, the strong performance of cell count alone on spatial transcriptomics makes it challenging to definitively prove how much marginal gain is attributable to spatial arrangement versus local density on real tissue samples.

strengths: Timely and high-impact sanity check for the burgeoning field of microscopy and bioimaging foundation models, paralleling recent eye-opening benchmark revelations in single-cell transcriptomics.

Comprehensive and well-chosen diagnostic baselines (pixel-level statistics, single-layer random convolutions, untrained deep networks, cell counts, and binarized cell graphs) that clearly expose what fraction of performance is attributable to inductive biases and low-level artifacts rather than learned biological semantics.

Broad empirical evaluation covering two major organizational scales in bioimaging: cell culture (RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, JUMP-MoA) and tissue histopathology / spatial transcriptomics (HEST-1k, BRACS, BACH).

Insightful mechanistic diagnoses, particularly the PCA effective dimensionality analysis explaining why untrained ViTs succeed while ResNets collapse, and the layer-wise analysis contrasting natural image depth progression with bioimaging representations.
Constructive and actionable recommendations for benchmark design, quality control, and baseline reporting to guide future research.
weaknesses: Evaluations are restricted to frozen feature representations (retrieval, ridge regression, and linear probing); while this is the standard paradigm for foundation model benchmarking, the study does not evaluate whether full fine-tuning or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) would reveal larger differences between pretrained and untrained models.

As acknowledged by the authors, the strongest in-domain cell models (e.g., MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8) are proprietary, precluding identical layer-wise and architectural probes on the top-performing representations.

On the tissue level, the causal mechanism behind the success of the cell-graph structure baselines remains partially confounded with local cell count, as shown in Appendix D.3; conditioning or matching on cell density across all benchmarks would strengthen the claim that spatial layout specifically drives the performance.
Minor presentation flaws and typos in the manuscript (e.g., 'generally generally true' on page 8, 'make strong about' on page 44, and several placeholder citation years such as 2026).

strengths: Timely and critical inquiry: As foundation models proliferate in computational pathology and cell biology, this paper provides a much-needed critical examination of what current bioimaging benchmarks actually measure, following similar impactful benchmark sanity-checks in transcriptomics.

Comprehensive empirical scope across biological scales: The evaluation spans both cellular-level assays (Cell Painting on RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP, and JUMP-MoA) and tissue-level assays (spatial transcriptomics on HEST-1k/HEST-1k-1NN and histology classification on BRACS and BACH), complemented by ImageNet-1k as a natural image reference.

Rigorous and revealing baseline design: The inclusion of pixel statistics, untrained/randomly initialized CNNs (including SingleConv) and ViTs, handcrafted morphology (CellProfiler), and structure-only representations (cell centroid graphs and cell counts) provides crucial calibration. The finding that a 1-layer random conv or untrained ViT matches OpenPhenom on RxRx3-core is a striking result.

Insightful diagnostic analyses: The paper goes beyond top-line numbers by diagnosing why ResNets fail (representational collapse into low-dimensional subspaces via PCA), demonstrating high ranking correlations between untrained and pretrained ViTs (Spearman rho ~ 0.7-0.8), and evaluating layer-wise dynamics (showing non-monotonic or plateauing behavior in deeper layers for bioimaging compared to natural images).

High reproducibility and thorough reporting: Experiments are conducted across multiple seeds and stratified cross-validation folds, with comprehensive documentation in the appendix and public data/code.
weaknesses: Predominantly diagnostic without constructive benchmark reform: While Section 5.3 outlines sensible benchmarking design principles, the paper does not concretely introduce, validate, or standardize an alternative benchmark suite or filtering methodology specifically designed to prevent low-level and cell-count shortcuts.

Confounding of spatial structure with simple cell counts: As the authors honestly acknowledge in Section 5.4 and Appendix D.3, the competitive performance of structure-only graph representations on HEST-1k is largely mimicked by a simple 1D non-linear cell count baseline. The study does not fully isolate whether higher-order spatial arrangement provides meaningful predictive signal beyond local cell density in real tissue samples.

Incomplete probing of state-of-the-art proprietary models: The highest-performing models on RxRx3-core (MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8) outperform the untrained baselines by 1.5x (Appendix G), but because their weights are proprietary, they could not be subjected to the layer-wise probing or representational similarity analyses. This somewhat tempers the broader conclusion regarding whether sufficiently scaled, domain-specific foundation models truly fail to learn high-level abstractions.

Heuristic nature of the cell graph image baseline: Rendering 5-NN cell centroid graphs as 224x224 binary images and passing them through an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet is a somewhat ad-hoc bridge between structure and standard vision encoders; while GCN and EGNN are also tested, their performance on synthetic vs. real tissue data shows inconsistent pretraining transfer.

strengths: Crucial and timely diagnostic contribution: Parallel to recent sanity-check findings in single-cell transcriptomics, this work rigorously tests whether microscopy foundation models learn high-level biological abstractions or merely exploit dataset shortcuts and architectural inductive biases.

Well-conceived baseline taxonomy: The inclusion of pixel-level intensity statistics, untrained randomly initialized vision encoders (including a minimal SingleConv baseline), and disentangled tissue-structure baselines (rendered cell graphs and GNNs) provides an essential calibration framework for microscopy benchmarks.

Compelling and surprising empirical findings: The observation that untrained ViTs and single-layer random CNNs match or rival pretrained foundation models like OpenPhenom on RxRx3-core gene retrieval—and share high Spearman correlation in ranking—is a striking revelation for the community.

Comprehensive analytical depth: Beyond reporting scalar benchmark numbers, the authors dissect representational behavior through intermediate-layer probing, Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), PCA variance/spectrum analysis to diagnose representational collapse in ResNets, and controlled synthetic experiments.

Nuanced and grounded conclusions: The manuscript avoids hyperbolic generalizations, carefully distinguishing settings where pretrained foundation models exhibit genuine learned abstractions (e.g., subtle phenotypes in JUMP-CP, deeper layer progression in H-Optimus-1 on HEST-1k, and scaled private MAEs) from settings dominated by low-level correlates.
weaknesses: Disentangling cell count from spatial arrangement in tissue imaging: As acknowledged in Section 5.3, the hand-crafted cell-counting baseline is remarkably competitive on HEST-1k / HEST-1k-1NN. While synthetic benchmarks control for node count, the extent to which graph representations on real tissue reflect complex spatial topology versus local nuclei density/count remains partially confounded.

Input channel adaptation for RGB-pretrained models: Adapting RGB vision backbones to 5- or 6-channel Cell Painting data via filter duplication/expansion could disadvantage out-of-domain pretrained models relative to architectures natively trained on multi-channel data, though OpenPhenom provides a partial control.

Subsampling protocol on RxRx3-core: The subsampling to 10 images per gene in the main text evaluation may disproportionately penalize pretrained embeddings whose advantage relies on aggregating noise across large replicate pools, although Appendix H provides full-dataset context.

Visual legibility in main text figures: Figures 1, 2, and 3 suffer from tiny font sizes and cramped layouts in the main text, requiring readers to frequently consult Appendix I for legible, upscaled plots.

strengths: Timely and critical contribution: The paper addresses a vital question in biological machine learning by interrogating what microscopy foundation models actually learn versus what is explainable by low-level statistical artifacts and architectural inductive biases.

Well-conceived and revealing baselines: Introducing pixel-level statistics, untrained/randomly initialized networks (including SingleConv), and disentangled tissue structure representations (cell-centroid graphs and point clouds) provides an effective calibration framework for microscopy benchmarks.

Rigorous and comprehensive empirical analysis: The authors evaluate multiple architectures (CNNs, ViTs, GNNs) across two foundational biological scales (Cell Painting on RxRx3-core and JUMP-CP; spatial transcriptomics on HEST-1k), including layer-wise probing, representational similarity analysis, and dimensionality diagnostics.

Compelling and surprising findings: The paper convincingly demonstrates that untrained ViTs and single-layer convolutions can match pretrained foundation models on gene-gene retrieval tasks, share high rank correlation with trained models, and that cell spatial organization/counts alone explain a large portion of spatial gene expression prediction.

Nuanced and intellectually honest discussion: The authors do not overclaim; they openly discuss the superior performance of proprietary large-scale models (MAE-L/8, MAE-G/8), delineate the role of cell counting versus cellular arrangement, and carefully distinguish between collapse checks and biological semantics.
weaknesses: Legibility of figures in the main text: Figures 1, 2, and 3 suffer from cramped layouts and tiny axis/legend fonts, forcing the reader to consult the appendix for readable versions (e.g., Figures 24 and 25).

Analysis of top-performing foundation models is limited by access: Because state-of-the-art models like MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8 remain private, internal layer-wise probing and mechanistic verification could not be performed on the models that actually demonstrate significant margins over the untrained baselines.

Cell count confounding in structure models: While synthetic experiments attempt to decouple cell count from spatial arrangement, the real-tissue experiments on HEST-1k/HEST-1k-1NN remain partially confounded by local cell density/count, leaving open whether the graph encoders genuinely learn tissue architecture rather than acting as non-linear cell counters.

Minor presentation polish: Several small typographical errors are present in the text (e.g., 'fonda-tion models' on page 2, duplicated phrasing 'used are used' on page 17, and 'generally generally' on page 29).

strengths: Critically needed reality check: The paper provides a timely, rigorous, and sober assessment of what microscopy foundation models actually learn, paralleling recent eye-opening findings in single-cell transcriptomics regarding benchmark shortcuts and over-optimistic evaluation.

Well-designed diagnostic baselines: The introduction of untrained/randomly initialized architectures (including a minimal SingleConv baseline), pixel statistics, cell counts, and structure-only graph/point-cloud views allows clear disentanglement between learned biological abstraction, low-level visual artifacts, and architectural inductive biases.

Compelling empirical findings: The observation that untrained ViTs and single-layer random conv nets rival foundation models on RxRx3-core gene-gene retrieval (with Spearman correlation ~0.8 between their prediction rankings) is striking and reveals fundamental issues in current high-throughput screening evaluation protocols.

Comprehensive multi-scale evaluation: The study covers both cell-level (RxRx3-core, JUMP-CP) and tissue-level (HEST-1k, HEST-1k-1NN) benchmarks, alongside intermediate-layer depth analyses, representational similarity analyses (RSA), and effective dimensionality/PCA collapse diagnostics.

Balanced and nuanced interpretation: The authors do not simply dismiss foundation models; they carefully delineate where foundation models truly add value (e.g., in-domain models like H-Optimus-1 on specific cancers, or private MAE-G models on RxRx3) versus where benchmark scores are inflated by cell density, counting, or architectural priors.
weaknesses: Figure readability and presentation flaws in the main text: Figures 1, 2, 3, and 4 in the main body are extremely small and difficult to read without zooming into the appendix versions. Additionally, there are minor labeling inconsistencies (e.g., Figure 3 y-axis is labeled 'Recall' while the caption and text discuss mAP; Figure 23 y-axis is labeled 'ImageNet Retrieval (mAP)' while showing JUMP-CP compound retrieval).

Missing comparison to standard classical cell profiling features: While pixel statistics and deep features are probed, incorporating classical CellProfiler morphological profiles (the standard non-deep baseline widely used in high-content screening) on RxRx3 and JUMP-CP would have made the cellular benchmarking baseline comparison even more comprehensive.

Diagnostic rather than prescriptive: While the paper thoroughly exposes the limitations of existing benchmarks and metrics, it does not propose a concrete new benchmark metric or training regularization objective to prevent models from learning these shortcuts, leaving this to future work.
